draft.title: Conjugate acid-base pairs
card: In the Brønsted-Lowry model, an acid donates a proton (H⁺) and a base accepts one. When an acid donates a proton, the species left behind is its conjugate base.
The reverse also works. When a base accepts a proton, it becomes its conjugate acid. A conjugate pair differs by exactly one H⁺.
Example: HCl donates a proton to become Cl⁻, so Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of HCl. NH₃ accepts a proton to become NH₄⁺, so NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of NH₃.
The stronger an acid is, the weaker its conjugate base. A strong acid gives up its proton very readily, so its conjugate base has very little attraction for a proton.
draft.remember: Conjugate partners differ by one H⁺. A strong acid has a very weak conjugate base.

a.q: What is the conjugate base of the hydrogen carbonate ion, HCO₃⁻?
opts: CO₃²⁻
H₂CO₃
H₂O
CO₂
a.why: A conjugate base is what is left after the acid donates one H⁺, so HCO₃⁻ becomes CO₃²⁻. H₂CO₃ is tempting, but it has gained a proton, so it is the conjugate acid of HCO₃⁻.
a.clue: Remove one H⁺ from the formula and adjust the charge.

b.q: Nitric acid, HNO₃, is a strong acid. What does this tell you about its conjugate base, NO₃⁻, in water?
opts: It is a very weak base with little attraction for H⁺
It is a strong base that readily accepts H⁺
It is a strong base because the acid is strong
It is neither an acid nor a base, so it cannot react
b.why: A strong acid gives up its proton very readily, so its conjugate base has very little attraction for H⁺ and is very weak. The tempting answer is a strong base, which reverses the link: strength in an acid goes with weakness in its conjugate base.
b.clue: A strong acid lets go of its proton easily.

b.best: It is a very weak base with little attraction for H⁺

problems.detail: The first bullet restates the Brønsted-Lowry definition (acid donates a proton, base accepts one), which belongs to point 2. It could simply refer to it as already learned rather than define it again.
